query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting roughly 10 at.% of Fe or Ni with Mo in an equiatomic FeCoNi high‐entropy alloy will introduce sufficient lattice distortion to enhance local magnetocrystalline anisotropy and create stronger domain‐wall pinning sites, thereby increasing the coercivity relative to the baseline soft ferromagnetic derivatives that incorporate Pd or Pt.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with an fcc structure, high saturation magnetization, and low coercive field (as observed in alloys like FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt).
generation.intervention: Replace approximately 10 at.% of either Fe or Ni with Mo while maintaining an almost equiatomic overall composition and high configurational entropy (≥1.0R).
generation.conditions: The alloy must be processed to preserve its fcc phase and equiatomic chemical composition, with testing conducted under standard ambient conditions (e.g., room temperature magnetometry) to assess magnetic properties.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions (possibly incipient tetragonal distortions) and associated strain fields in the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Mo, possessing a different atomic radius and electronic structure than Fe, Co, and Ni, leads to moderate lattice distortions when substituted into the alloy. These distortions enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy and generate local strain fields that act as effective pinning sites for magnetic domain walls, which in turn increases the coercivity of the material.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-modified alloy will exhibit a higher coercive field while retaining high saturation magnetization, representing a transition from soft to harder ferromagnetic behavior compared to the baseline FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt alloys.
generation.baseline: The FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys with Pd or Pt additions that, despite high configurational entropy and equiatomic compositions, display low coercivity (soft ferromagnetism).
generation.boundary: This effect is expected when the Mo substitution is maintained around 10 at.% without triggering secondary phase formation or significantly altering the fcc structure; deviations beyond this range may compromise either the magnetic or phase-stability characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the coercivity increase is uncertain and may depend on the precise level of Mo substitution and processing conditions. Fine-tuning of the Mo content may be required to optimize the balance between increased coercivity and retention of high saturation magnetization and phase stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two series of alloys: one series of baseline FeCoNi-based high‐entropy alloys (e.g., FeCoNiPd or FeCoNiPt) and another series where approximately 10 at.% of Fe or Ni is replaced with Mo, ensuring all samples remain nearly equiatomic and fcc. Under identical processing conditions, carry out room temperature magnetic hysteresis measurements to collect coercivity and saturation magnetization data. Additionally, perform X-ray diffraction to verify that the fcc structure and lattice distortion are preserved.
measurements: Magnetic hysteresis loops to extract coercive fields
X-ray diffraction for phase analysis and detection of lattice distortions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-substituted alloy does not show a statistically significant higher coercivity (beyond a predetermined threshold relative to the baseline) while maintaining the fcc structure and high saturation magnetization, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

decision.trend: The early work on high‐entropy alloys in the Fe–Co–Ni family (and the closely related CrMnFeCoNi systems) has focused on maintaining equiatomic compositions with high configurational entropy and an fcc structure. Early interventions – for example, substituting Pd or Pt into FeCoNi to form FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt – successfully kept the configurational entropy at or above 1.0R and preserved the high saturation magnetization, but these alloys remained soft ferromagnets with low coercivity. Similar studies on other equiatomic fcc HEAs have shown that while the high‐entropy design confers excellent phase stability and mechanical properties, the magnetic anisotropy and domain‐wall pinning mechanisms have not been sufficiently enhanced to yield hard magnetic behavior.
decision.unsolved: The persistent open question is how to increase coercivity without sacrificing the equiatomic, high‐entropy nature of the alloy. Although noble metal additions (Pd, Pt) meet the thermodynamic and compositional criteria, they do not introduce the lattice distortions or local anisotropies necessary to strengthen the pinning of magnetic domains. In short, the mechanism leading to a harder (higher coercivity) magnetic response remains unsolved.
decision.lever: Introduce a moderate substitution of a 3d transition metal element (e.g., replacing ~10 at.% of Fe or Ni with Mo) into the FeCoNi matrix
decision.why: Mo, with its smaller atomic radius and distinct electronic structure relative to the base elements, is expected to induce a slight lattice distortion (or even a subtle tendency toward a tetragonally distorted phase) within the fcc matrix. This distortion enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy and creates local strain fields that act as effective domain‐wall pinning centers. Such a compositional tweak follows the trend of modifying alloy compositions to tune physical properties and directly addresses the coercivity gap observed in the earlier Pd and Pt derivatives. The hypothesis can be experimentally tested by comparing the hysteresis loops of the Mo–modified FeCoNi alloy with the baseline; a clear increase in coercivity (beyond a predetermined threshold) would support the proposal, whereas failure to observe significant enhancement would falsify it.
